claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase FCC/B2 lamellar microstructure.
Eutectic high-entropy alloys of this type have limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups near phase boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure during straining.
Rolling followed by phase-selective annealing can increase ductility while retaining or increasing strength.
Annealing at approximately 650–750 °C for 30–60 minutes after cold or cryogenic rolling will partially recrystallize the soft FCC lamellae.
A rolling reduction of approximately 8–40% at or below room temperature is an applicable preprocessing range for the proposed treatment.
The intermediate anneal will preserve relatively fine B2 regions.
Localized FCC recrystallization disrupts dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces.
Phase-selective FCC recrystallization mitigates stress concentrations associated with internal boundaries.
Recrystallized grains in the ductile phase accommodate strain more uniformly and increase strain-hardening capacity.
More uniform strain accommodation prevents interfacial microcracking and catastrophic failure.
The unrecrystallized hard B2 phase acts as a barrier and maintains the alloy's overall load-bearing capacity.
The proposed partially recrystallized material can achieve approximately 25% or greater room-temperature elongation to failure.
The proposed treatment can retain or surpass a baseline yield strength of approximately 1–1.2 GPa and potentially produce strengths of 1.2–2.0 GPa.
Untreated as-cast material generally has room-temperature tensile ductility near 10–15%.
Untreated as-cast material generally has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1–1.2 GPa.
Excessively high annealing temperatures or long annealing times can coarsen B2 lamellae or cause over-recrystallization and thereby reduce strength.
The optimal annealing temperature and duration depend on alloy composition and rolling reduction.
